title: GPX Merger: Combine Tracks Into One File
description: Merge GPX files in your browser with the GPX Merger — tracks, routes and waypoints combined, each source preserved as its own element. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, three day-files of 48 KB, 120 KB and 35 KB combine into one 203 KB archive of the trip — every track still separate inside, nothing stitched into a fake continuous line.
quick_answer: The GPX Merger combines tracks, routes and waypoints from two or more GPX files into a single file, locally in your browser, keeping each source element separate. Drop the files and download the union — one trip archive instead of fragments, without pretending separate outings were continuous.

body.t: A week of day-files becomes the trip's single GPX — the file you share, back up and load into the
Watch file plus phone backup plus the route you planned: three sources, one document, each part still identifiable.
A club's season of hikes merged per-region gives newcomers one download per area instead of forty fragments.
Analyzers that take one file get the merged union — point counts, boxes and spans then describe the whole set at once.

File A's morning track and file B's evening track enter the merge as two <trk> elements. A viewer draws both; a stats tool sums both; nobody's software draws a phantom straight line from the morning's end to the evening's start across the lunch break.
Campsites saved on the phone, summits from the watch, the bothy from a friend's file: waypoints pool into one <wpt> set — the trip's gazetteer in a single document.

popular_table.note: Nothing is resampled, re-timed or re-ordered within an element — merging changes the container, not the recordings. Duplicate points across overlapping files remain duplicates; cleaning is the deduplication family's job.

faq: In what order do elements appear?
By source file, in the order you add them — each file's contents intact. Chronology inside the merged file follows your file order, so add day-files in date order for a tidy archive.
They coexist; GPX readers distinguish tracks by position and content, not only by name. Rename before merging if your library software sorts by name.
Trackpoints carry their extension data with them — the channels survive merging because the points themselves are copied whole.
One file ends where another begins — joined?
No: proximity is not stitched. Two tracks that happen to touch remain two tracks, which is the truth of how they were recorded.
As many as your browser's memory comfortably holds — a season of ordinary recordings is fine; a decade of 1-second tracks belongs to desktop tooling.
No — every stamp is copied as recorded. If the sources disagree about clocks, that was true before the merge and stays visible after.
